title: Why Valles de Benavente tastes the way it does

lede.text: Prieto Picudo ripens in an arid climate with very cold winters, on poor soil that drains well. The wines come out red-fruited, often with a slight spritz the locals call aguja.

chapters.title: Where the Esla meets the Órbigo
paras: The vineyards lie in the north-east of Zamora province. They cover 1,520 km² across 62 municipalities, mostly in the valleys of four rivers: the Esla, the Tera, the Órbigo and the Eria.

Benavente sits at about 740 m, where the Órbigo meets the Esla. That altitude differs by around 80-100 m from the Prieto Picudo country of León, and it makes Benavente's climate 3 or 4 degrees less cold.

Wine here is old business. In 1338 King Alfonso XI confirmed a town rule that banned outside wine from Benavente. The town had a great stretch of vineyards and enough wine of its own for the whole year.

chapters.title: Long cold winters, short dry summers
paras: The climate is continental, extreme and arid, with 350-550 mm of rain a year. Winters are very cold, with a long frost season and fog that lingers.
Summers are dry, hot and short. Nights cool down sharply, which softens the heat of the day. The vines still get the water they need, and the wines gain colour, freshness and balanced acidity.
Prieto Picudo buds early and is very sensitive to spring frost.

chapters.title: Poor soil that drains
paras: The typical soils are brown and limestone-rich. They are sandy loam, with a pH between 7 and 8, and 50-60 cm deep. Fertility is low, but they drain and aerate so well that they suit the vine.
Rain soaks in easily. In places the land turns to clay plains where drainage is very slow.
Some Prieto Picudo vines are old, between 70 and 80 years. That age gives the grapes the quality for wines meant to be kept.

chapters.title: Prieto Picudo sets the tone
paras: Prieto Picudo is the signature grape. Its berries are small and its bunches very compact. The thick skin gives a strong tannic structure, red fruit, sweet soft tannins and balanced acidity.
Old cellar practice here made wines with a little spritz, called aguja. It still marks the wines, and some rosados show it today.
Reds must hold at least 75% of the main red varieties: Prieto Picudo, Tempranillo or Mencía. Reds are limited to 7,000 kg per hectare and whites to 9,000 kg.
Nearby León uses a technique called madreo. Benavente does not, and that makes the wines of the two zones completely different.
Aged reds gain wood and complexity, but the fruit stays. Ageing is counted from 1 November of the harvest year.

terms.text: A traditional term that may stand on the label in place of "Denominación de Origen Protegida".
